newsitem.title: UK: FX in Europe - Dlr falters in thin, jittery market.
newsitem.headline: FX in Europe - Dlr falters in thin, jittery market.

text.p: The dollar ended the European trading session almost three pfennigs and nearly one yen lower as players liquidated some long positions ahead of a week packed with key events, traders said.
Thin trading, with many European markets shut for a holiday, exaggerated movements. The dollar came under fierce pressure at the U.S. open as hedge funds and corporates liquidated longs.
"The dollar had been on a downward trend all day and when some big sellers came into the market as the U.S. opened, it accelerated," said Peter von Maydell, FX strategist at UBS.
At 1520 GMT the dollar was at 1.8178/88 marks, close to session lows and down from 1.8440/50 in late Europe on Thursday.
Against the yen it was at 117.00/10, off a low at 116.85 but well below a two-week peak at 118.70 and down from 117.80/85 at the previous European close.
Dollar/yen reversed some of its gains made in the wake of receding Japanese rate rise expectations and concern about the impact of the South East Asian FX crisis on Japanese economy.
Speculation about a German rate rise has intensified after the Bundesbank said on Wednesday it was concerned about inflation and would steer policy to maintain price stability.
The Bundesbank's next money market operations are on Tuesday and its policy-making council meets for the first time after the summer recess on Thursday.
"The market's appetite to sell marks has weakened on it's nervous going into next week," said a trader at a U.S. bank.

The Bundesbank has spent much of its summer recess to sending signals to the market that the next rate move will be up to give itself scope to act at short notice. "The Bundesbank is keeping a sword hanging over the market," said Ulrich Beckmann, economist at Deutsche Bank Research in Frankfurt.
Many analysts expect the Bundesbank to hold fire next week and wait with a rate rise until later to prevent damage to the economic recovery in Germany.
"It can achieve more with the threat of action than with action itself," said Beckmann.

The latest hawkish comments came from Bundesbank vice-president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum who said in an interview published late on Thursday said the bank was concerned about domestic price pressures in the pipeline and that it wanted "full scope to act."
"It didn't have much of a net impact on the dollar but the signs are all in the same direction," said the U.S. bank trader.
Dollar/yen is likely to be underpinned by worries that the South East Asian currency crisis might hurt Japanese exporters and threaten the fragile economic recovery.
"The actual impact on Japan is likely to be small but it has had a very big influence on sentiment for dollar/yen," said von Maydell.
The latest victim of the crisis was the Indonesian rupiah, which tumbled to record lows against the dollar after it was floated on Thursday.

"There's a general trend of Asian currencies showing a lot of volatility," said James Binney, fund manager at GNI in London. "As a result, their weakening makes the yen look rather overvalued ... and the yen needs to weaken for competitive reasons."

Analysts said the dollar was going to benefit from the Asian turmoil as much of the money flowing out of Asia was likely to go into the U.S. where the economy is performing much better than in Japan. A fall in the Japanese long bond's yield to a record low of 2.065 percent overnight highlighted the dollar's relative yield advantage over Japan.
Near-term direction for dollar/yen will also come from Japan's customs-cleared trade data for July, due out at 2350 GMT on Sunday.
Yen weakness across the board pushed the mark to a fresh two-week high at 64.65. In late trade it was at 64.47/52 from 63.87/90 at the close here on Thursday.
Sterling/yen surged above 190 before easing slightly to 189.75/99 in late trade here.
